Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007      Palladium  
CRU International Limited confidential 
Palladium 
 
Recent trends 
Palladium broke out of its trading range in a technically significant manner at the end of 2006, 
finally reaching $340/oz and then $350/oz by the end of January on the back of fresh fund 
buying and strong gains in platinum.  Like its sister metal, palladium too succumbed to the 
weakness in the equity markets in early March but (perhaps surprisingly) from a technical 
standpoint the weakness in this market was a lot less than had been registered in other PGMs.   
• Industrial end-users have been sidelined with palladium’s gradual move upwards and are 
waiting for a bigger correction than that which occurred in early March. 
• Despite palladium’s rather poor fundamental outlook, speculators have continued to take up 
long positions on NYMEX.  The net non-commercial long position increased by more than 
5,100 contracts (16 tonnes) since the end of 2006 to a high of 7,020 contracts (21.8 tonnes) 
on 13 March.  Though this position has since reduced by some 300 contracts, it is likely that 
the conspicuous lack of volatility has had a bearing on investor attitudes towards this metal, 
being an attractive quality to those looking for a long-term bull strategy. 
• Bullion imports of palladium into Zurich increased by 675% year-on-year in December 
2006.  While large imports of palladium from Russia into Switzerland at the beginning or 
end of the calendar year is not in itself an unusual occurrence, the scale of the increase last 
December served to underline the metal’s fundamental situation and temporarily inhibited 
it’s movement higher in line with the rest of the precious metals complex in February.   
• Total Russian shipments for the full year 2006 amounted to 5,026,172oz, up 36.5% 
compared with 2005.  This reflects the higher quantities of metal being exported to 
Switzerland and Hong Kong - trade data shows that, year-on-year, imports from Russia 
increased by 257% and 107% respectively.  Output at Norilsk increased by 31,000oz to 
3,164,000oz in 2006. 
• North American Palladium produced 73,242oz during 2006 Q4, up 99% compared with the 
corresponding period of 2005 due to improved mill feed grades and metal recovery.  Full 
year output for 2006 therefore increased by 34% to 237,388oz.

Precious Metals Quarterly 1Q2007    Palladium 
55 
Forecast update: investment demand key to 
maintaining prices 
Following huge growth in palladium jewellery offtake in China over 2004/05, the recycling of 
Pd950 stock put a dent in demand last year.  Further growth is now very much dependant on it’s 
popularity spreading to the primary cities and making an impact in other markets, such as the 
USA.  The sustained Pt-Pd price spread should help to drive offtake at the fashion end of the 
spectrum.  We believe that there is potential for substantial growth in this sector with effective 
marketing initiatives. 
 
The USA auto market looks to be stagnating with foreign manufacturers pulling the rug from 
under domestic producers (see Platinum Forecast Update).  CRU forecasts that autocatalytic 
demand for palladium in North America will grow by an annual average of less than 3% over 
the forecast period.  However, the demand outlook for China is very positive given the recent 
and projected growth in vehicle production.  This will offset weakness in the USA - global 
demand for palladium in autocats could exceed 5.3Moz by 2011. 
 
Trade data for 2006 highlights the fact that there are still ample stocks of palladium.  
Shipments from Russia totalled 59.7 tonnes in 2006, which is 249% higher compared with the 
year before.  The market is still reliant on Russian shipments; however, the country’s stockpile 
is a mere fraction of what it was a decade ago.  With less scope for large stock sales, this will 
help rein in the market surplus over the forecast period. 
 
Switzerland imported 40.1 tonnes of palladium from Russia in December 2006, bringing full 
year imports from Russia alone to 71.6 tonnes (the highest level since 2001).  Total imports for 
2006 amounted to 126.2 tonnes, up 174% on 2005, and with exports down by 35% year-on-year 
at 48.1 tonnes; implied inventories now stand just below 230 tonnes by our calculation.  Large 
inventories of palladium will likely prevent any sustained upward trend in prices, especially 
factoring in growth in primary and secondary supplies.  
 
Recovery of palladium from scrap is set to grow by a substantial rate over the forecast 
period, and could increase by almost 30% in 2007 alone as a result of the large number of cars 
built in the mid- to late-nineties (during which time palladium loading in autocatalysts 
increased, see Palladium Storyboard) that are now being scrapped.  Furthermore, mine 
production is forecast to exceed 8.5Moz by 2011. 
 
Palladium outperformed both platinum and gold over 2006, owing to its projected growth in 
jewellery demand and substitution for platinum in the autocat sector.  Investor interest was a 
key driver of prices, with market participants being attracted by low volatility but overlooking 
high inventories and increasing supplies.  This means that palladium is vulnerable to changes in 
sentiment, but with the platinum and gold markets expected to remain strong in the short- to 
medium-term; we do not expect prices to fall below $300/oz.   
 
CRU forecast’s a long-term average palladium price of $339/oz.
